frameworks.name: The Obsession Reframing
frameworks.definition: What others call obsession is actually sane behavior in a finite lifespan; normal people waste their lives while sane people maximize time for meaningful activity.

frameworks.name: Judgment as Preference Mismatch
frameworks.definition: All criticism reduces to one statement: 'You do not live your life in a way that I prefer.' Understanding this dissolves defensiveness and enables clarity about whose preferences matter.

frameworks.name: Jealousy as Desert Belief
frameworks.definition: When people hate on you, they believe life has unjustly given you benefits they rightfully deserve. The form of jealousy (attention, money, body) varies, but the mechanism is identical.

frameworks.name: Work-Life Balance as Mediocrity Signal
frameworks.definition: People obsessed with work-life balance are typically mediocre at both. Excellence requires applying obsession to everything and redefining 'life' to include the work.

frameworks.name: Smart vs Hard Work Competition
frameworks.definition: When competing against other smart people, work-smart-not-hard fails. The only differentiator is working both smart and hard.

claims.text: What people call obsession is actually just trying; normal people call sane people obsessed because sane people actually work while normal people do nothing and waste their lives.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: All insults and judgments reduce to one statement: 'You do not live your life in a way that I prefer.' When someone criticizes how you live, they are asserting a preference mismatch, not an objective truth.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Life has finite hours and a finite lifespan; given this constraint, the rational choice is to spend time on activities you prefer rather than compromising your preferences to satisfy others' opinions about how you should live.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: life has limited hours and you will die; spending those hours on things you do not prefer is irrational.

claims.text: When people hate on you, it usually signals jealousy: they believe you are undeserving of some part of your life that they themselves deserve. The form of jealousy varies—attention, money, body, status—but the mechanism is identical.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: life has given you a benefit the hater believes is rightfully theirs; the injustice they perceive drives the emotion.
bounded_by: not applicable to genuine constructive criticism from trusted sources

claims.text: People who obsess about work-life balance are typically mediocre at both; obsessed people apply their obsession to everything and call it life, without considering themselves obsessed.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: work-life balance is a wonderful goal for those not competing for the top; it is incompatible with being the best

claims.text: The criticism 'you don't have any hobbies' is asserting a preference: it means 'if I were in your position, I would live differently.' The response is: that is why you are not in my position.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Work smart, not hard only works when competing against people who are not smart. When competing against other smart people, the only remaining variable is effort; smart people who also work hard beat smart people who only work smart.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: in a peer-ability environment, the differentiator collapses to effort; effort becomes the binding constraint.
bounded_by: does not apply when competitors lack equivalent intelligence or work ethic

claims.text: Being the best requires sacrificing work-life balance. Excellence is incompatible with a balanced lifestyle because the required hours and intensity exceed what balance permits.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: if goal is to be the best
claims.mechanism: achieving the top 1% requires time and focus allocation that crowds out other activities; balance limits ceiling.

examples.text: A person criticizes: 'You work too much.' This criticism is shorthand for: 'I believe you are undeserving of the success you have, because I would choose a different life and you have chosen to work instead. I am jealous that you have the attention / money / body / status you have because I believe I deserve it more than you do.' The criticism itself is a confession of the critic's belief system, not a truth about the target.

Portfolio companies with founders who push hard and apply intense focus scale faster and to higher revenue than those with founders who balance work and life. The high-growth cohort did not separate work from life; they redefined life to include the work. The balanced-life cohort remained mediocre, claiming they had chosen family time and rest, not understanding that their choice locked them into a specific outcome ceiling.

practices.text: When criticized or hated, translate the statement to its reduction: 'You do not live your life in a way that I prefer.' Recognize this as a preference statement about the critic, not a truth about you. Respond by clarifying that you live your life, not theirs.

If you want to be the best at your domain, commit to hard work. Invest all available hours in the domain where you want to win. Do not negotiate or rationalize work-life balance when your goal is excellence.
